latent_mechanisms.display_name: EBV/CMV lytic replication in B cells and oropharyngeal epithelium
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Primary EBV (or less commonly CMV) infection drives lytic replication in pharyngeal B-lymphocytes and epithelium, generating viremia that seeds reticuloendothelial system and triggers all downstream immune activation in IM.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Waldeyer ring lymphoid hyperplasia and tonsillar exudate
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Massive proliferation of EBV-infected B cells and reactive T cells in tonsillar/adenoid tissue producing the exudative pharyngitis, palatal petechiae, and risk of upper airway obstruction.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Polyclonal CD8+ T cell expansion against EBV-infected B cells
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Massive CD8+ cytotoxic T cell response is the immunologic hallmark of IM; these are the morphologically atypical/reactive (Downey) lymphocytes, and their tissue infiltration drives most clinical features rather than direct viral cytopathology.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Polyclonal B-cell activation and heterophile antibody production
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: EBV-driven nonspecific B cell activation produces heterophile (Paul-Bunnell) antibodies, transient autoantibodies, cold agglutinins, and cryoglobulins; underlies the heterophile-positive serology and immune cytopenia risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic reticuloendothelial and lymphoid organ expansion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Reactive expansion of cervical/generalized lymph nodes, spleen, and liver from CD8 T-cell infiltration plus B-cell hyperplasia; substrate for lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and the splenic rupture hazard.

Sinusoidal CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration of the liver causes near-universal subclinical hepatitis (mild-moderate AST/ALT elevation, occasional cholestasis); fulminant hepatitis is rare except in XLP/immunodeficient hosts.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: IL-6 / acute phase cytokine response to EBV
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Moderate IL-6, IFN-γ, and TNF release driving fever, anorexia, malaise, and modest CRP/ferritin rise — distinctly less intense than bacterial sepsis or AOSD/MAS.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Immune-mediated cytopenia (AIHA, ITP, neutropenia) in IM
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Polyclonal B-cell activation generates anti-i cold agglutinins (AIHA) and antiplatelet antibodies (ITP); mild neutropenia is common, severe cytopenias are uncommon but recognized complications.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Impaired NK/CTL clearance of EBV-infected B cells
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Background substrate that, when severe (XLP, perforin/SAP/MUNC defects, prior immunosuppression), permits unchecked EBV-driven macrophage activation and HLH; in immunocompetent IM this is mostly low-level.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Macrophage activation pressure on EBV-driven HLH spectrum
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Spectrum activity ranging from mild ferritin/LDH elevation in ordinary IM to fulminant EBV-HLH in susceptible hosts; clinically tracked via ferritin, sIL-2R, fibrinogen, triglycerides, cytopenias.
Long-term latent activity relevant in immunocompromised hosts (PTLD, Burkitt, Hodgkin, NK/T-cell lymphoma) and in chronic active EBV; near-zero in immunocompetent IM.

Persistent fatigue, exercise intolerance, and impaired concentration after the acute phase resolves; mechanism likely sustained immune activation and central effects, lasts weeks-months in 10-30% of cases.

Activated CD8 milieu of IM markedly amplifies T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity; amoxicillin/ampicillin/cephalosporin exposure precipitates a generalized maculopapular rash in a high fraction of IM patients (classic teaching ~80-90%, modern estimates lower but still substantial).

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Initial EBV replication occurs in oropharyngeal B cells and tonsillar epithelium, directly driving Waldeyer ring hyperplasia and exudative pharyngitis.
Viral antigen presentation drives the massive oligoclonal CD8+ T-cell response that defines IM and produces the atypical lymphocytes.
EBV directly polyclonally stimulates B cells via LMP1/CD40-mimicry, producing heterophile antibodies and transient autoantibodies.
Innate sensing of EBV plus T-cell activation drive moderate IL-6/TNF/IFN-γ, producing fever and acute-phase response.
Active viral replication produces measurable plasma/whole-blood EBV DNA, peaking around symptom onset and declining over weeks.
Reactive CD8+ T cells appear morphologically as Downey atypical lymphocytes; >10% atypical lymphs is a classical IM finding.
Absolute and relative lymphocytosis (often >50% lymphs, ALC often >4-5 ×10^9/L) is a hallmark hematologic finding in IM.
Lymphocytosis usually elevates total WBC into the 10-20 ×10^9/L range; markedly higher counts should prompt consideration of leukemia/lymphoma.
Reactive T cells home to lymph nodes, spleen, and liver, driving organomegaly and lymphadenopathy.
CD8+ sinusoidal infiltration is the dominant histopathologic finding in IM hepatitis, not direct viral cytopathology.
Heterophile (Paul-Bunnell) IgM antibodies arise from polyclonal B-cell activation; positive in ~85-90% of adolescents/adults with EBV-IM, lower in young children.
VCA-IgM appears within 1-2 weeks of symptom onset and persists 4-8 weeks; specific marker of acute primary EBV.
VCA-IgG appears soon after VCA-IgM and persists lifelong; useful for past infection.
EBNA-IgG appears 6-12 weeks to several months after onset; absence in the setting of VCA-IgM-positive serology supports acute primary infection.
Tonsillar hyperplasia and inflammation produce severe odynophagia, often the most prominent presenting symptom.
Thick gray-white exudates over enlarged tonsils are classic; clinically indistinguishable from streptococcal exudate without testing.
Petechiae at the junction of hard and soft palate are a relatively specific physical sign of IM (~25-30% of cases).

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Severe in young children and patients with massive tonsillar enlargement
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Massive tonsillar hyperplasia can cause upper airway obstruction; rare but a key indication for corticosteroids and observation/intubation.
Symmetric posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is most characteristic; generalized lymphadenopathy is common.
Palpable splenomegaly in ~50% clinically and ~100% by imaging; substrate for splenic rupture.
Tender hepatomegaly is present in ~10-20% clinically; imaging detection is higher.
Bilateral upper-eyelid (Hoagland sign) and periorbital edema is an early, relatively specific finding in IM (~25-30% of cases).

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Especially with contact sports, abdominal trauma, or Valsalva
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Spontaneous or trauma-associated splenic rupture occurs in ~0.1-0.5% of IM, almost exclusively in the first 3-4 weeks; highest mortality complication.
ALT typically rises 2-5×ULN in 80-90% of IM; >10×ULN suggests alternative or complicating cause.
AST tracks with ALT; pattern is hepatocellular.
Mild ALP elevation common; cholestatic pattern with bilirubin elevation occurs in a minority.
Mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from cholestatic component; overt jaundice signals more severe disease.
LDH elevation reflects lymphocyte turnover and hepatocyte injury; commonly 1.5-3×ULN.
Fever 38-40°C is near-universal in adolescent/adult IM, often persists 1-2 weeks; fever beyond 3 weeks should prompt re-evaluation.
Tachycardia tracks fever and dehydration in acute IM; usually resolves with defervescence.
CRP rises modestly in IM (often 20-100 mg/L); markedly higher CRP should raise concern for bacterial coinfection (peritonsillar abscess, streptococcal pharyngitis).
Profound fatigue and malaise dominate the clinical picture; persists into convalescence via post_viral_fatigue_activity.
Persistent fatigue lasting weeks to months after acute symptoms resolve; classic counseling point for adolescent and college-age patients.
Cold agglutinins (anti-i) and antiplatelet antibodies generated during polyclonal B-cell activation are the basis of IM-associated AIHA and ITP.
Anti-i cold-agglutinin AIHA produces a transient hemolytic anemia with elevated reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, positive DAT (C3d).
Mild thrombocytopenia is common; severe ITP is rare but reported, occasionally requiring corticosteroids/IVIg.
Mild-to-moderate neutropenia (often around 1.0-1.5 ×10^9/L) is common in IM and resolves spontaneously.
Mild ferritin elevation is common in ordinary IM; markedly elevated ferritin (>10,000 ng/mL) should prompt evaluation for EBV-HLH.
Failure of NK/CTL clearance of EBV-infected B cells permits unchecked macrophage activation, the defining mechanism of EBV-HLH.
EBV is the most common viral trigger for secondary HLH; recognition triggers urgent etoposide-based protocols.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Chronic active EBV, post-transplant, HIV, congenital immunodeficiency
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: EBV-driven B-cell or T/NK-cell lymphoproliferative disease; outside the scope of immunocompetent IM but essential for differential during prolonged or atypical course.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Aminopenicillin or selected cephalosporin exposure during acute IM
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Generalized morbilliform rash arises 5-10 days after antibiotic exposure; benign, self-limited, not a true type I allergy and does not contraindicate future use outside acute IM.
Background mortality in immunocompetent IM is extremely low (<0.1%); mortality clusters around splenic rupture, airway obstruction, fulminant hepatitis, and EBV-HLH.
Splenic rupture is the leading single cause of death in IM via hemorrhagic shock; emergency laparotomy or angioembolization is life-saving.
Severe upper airway obstruction can cause asphyxia if not promptly managed with corticosteroids, observation, and airway intervention.
EBV-HLH carries 30-50% mortality without prompt etoposide-based therapy and is a leading mortality driver outside ordinary IM.
Rare but well-described, typically in immunocompromised hosts; presents with marked hyperbilirubinemia, INR elevation, encephalopathy.

axes.shape_free_text: Sustained fever 38-40°C lasting 1-2 weeks, gradual lysis; persistence beyond 3 weeks is atypical and should trigger re-evaluation.
Tachycardia tracking fever and volume status, normalizes with defervescence.
Mild-to-moderate leukocytosis driven by lymphocytosis; typically 10-20, occasionally up to 25.
Marked lymphocytosis, typically 4-10 ×10^9/L, often with >50% lymphs on differential.
Reactive/atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells); >0.10 is highly suggestive of IM, often 0.20-0.40.
Mild neutropenia common; nadir typically 1.0-2.0 ×10^9/L.
Mild thrombocytopenia common (~50% of cases), severe ITP rare.
Usually preserved; falls only with AIHA complication.
Elevated only in AIHA subset.
Decreases only in AIHA subset.
C3d-positive DAT in IM-associated cold AIHA.
Mild-moderate elevation, typically 2-5×ULN, peaks week 2-3, normalizes over 4-8 weeks.
Tracks ALT, hepatocellular pattern.
Mildly elevated; cholestatic spike in jaundiced subset.
Usually normal; 5-10% of adults develop visible jaundice.
Commonly 1.5-3×ULN, reflects lymphocyte turnover and hepatocyte injury.
Modest rise (typically 20-100 mg/L); markedly higher CRP raises concern for bacterial coinfection.
Mild elevation in ordinary IM; markedly elevated values prompt EBV-HLH workup.
Monospot positive within 1-2 weeks of symptoms in ~85-90% of adolescents/adults; positivity wanes over months. Lower sensitivity in young children and CMV-IM.
VCA-IgM appears within 1-2 weeks of symptom onset, persists 4-8 weeks; specific marker of acute primary EBV.
VCA-IgG appears in acute phase and persists lifelong.
EBNA-IgG appears 6-12 weeks to several months after onset; absence with VCA-IgM positivity supports acute primary EBV.
Plasma/whole-blood EBV DNA detectable in acute primary infection, peaking near symptom onset and declining over weeks; persistently very high values raise concern for HLH or EBV-LPD.
Severe odynophagia is a defining presenting feature; usually resolves over 7-14 days.
Bilateral gray-white exudates over enlarged tonsils.
Pinpoint petechiae at junction of hard and soft palate; transient and relatively specific.
Bilateral, often tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is most characteristic; generalized adenopathy is also common.
Splenomegaly peaks in week 2-3; spleen is fragile during this period and is the substrate for splenic rupture.
Mild tender hepatomegaly in a minority of cases; correlates with ALT elevation.
Bilateral upper eyelid (Hoagland sign) and periorbital edema, early and relatively specific.
Profound malaise dominates the acute phase; persistent post-IM fatigue lasts weeks-months in 10-30%.
Mild diffuse myalgia early in illness.
Frontal/global headache common in early phase.
Spontaneous rash in 5-15%; iatrogenic aminopenicillin-associated morbilliform rash in a high fraction of treated cases.
Hazard concentrated in weeks 1-4; risk falls sharply once splenomegaly resolves.
Highest at peak tonsillar hyperplasia; mitigated by corticosteroids in selected cases.
Rare; clusters in immunocompromised hosts and XLP.
Substantially elevated in immunocompromised and XLP; very low in immunocompetent IM.
Overall mortality <0.1% in immunocompetent IM; concentrated in splenic rupture, airway obstruction, fulminant hepatitis, and EBV-HLH.
Positive in CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative IM-like syndrome).
Detectable in CMV mononucleosis; key in immunocompromised differentiation.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Atypical fraction and absolute lymphocyte count both reflect the same CD8 expansion mechanism and rise together, but the atypical fraction is a more specific IM marker.
ALT and AST track together in mononucleosis hepatitis (hepatocellular pattern).
Both rise during acute primary EBV but heterophile is less sensitive (especially in young children); discordance — heterophile-negative with VCA-IgM-positive — is informative.
Splenic enlargement and capsular thinning in weeks 1-4 produce the rupture-vulnerable substrate.
Viral load peaks first, then antibody response follows; explains the small early window where PCR is positive but serology is not.
Ferritin >10,000 ng/mL has high specificity for HLH; ferritin trend is a useful early warning.
EBNA-IgG seroconversion lags VCA-IgM by 6-12+ weeks; their joint pattern enables staging of primary vs past EBV infection.
Severe tonsillar enlargement with kissing tonsils precedes airway compromise.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: In significant IM hepatitis, dose-cap or prefer alternative analgesia; acetaminophen at therapeutic doses is generally safe but caution at high cumulative doses.

side_effects.interpretation: minimal at therapeutic doses; toxicity at supratherapeutic dosing

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line antipyretic and analgesic for fever and odynophagia in IM.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NSAID inhibition of platelet function adds to IM-associated thrombocytopenia and increases bleeding risk.
Increased bleeding risk if splenic rupture occurs; many clinicians prefer acetaminophen during peak splenomegaly.

treatments.context_specific_role: Useful for fever and pain; avoid or use cautiously with thrombocytopenia or large splenomegaly.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Corticosteroids rapidly reduce tonsillar hyperplasia and are first-line for impending airway compromise.
Component of HLH-directed therapy alongside etoposide.
Avoid empiric steroids in undifferentiated febrile illness without IM confirmation; can worsen unrecognized bacterial sepsis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reserved for impending airway obstruction, severe immune cytopenia (AIHA, ITP), neurologic complications, fulminant hepatitis, or as part of HLH therapy. Not recommended for routine uncomplicated IM.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Modest, not standalone; case-based use in EBV-HLH and chronic active EBV alongside immunosuppression.

failure_modes: no clinical benefit in routine IM despite reduced oropharyngeal shedding

side_effects.interpretation: crystal nephropathy risk if poorly hydrated

treatments.context_specific_role: Not indicated for uncomplicated IM (no clinical benefit shown); occasionally considered in selected severe/complicated EBV disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Backbone of treatment for EBV-driven post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease and selected EBV-HLH.
HBV screening and prophylaxis required prior to use.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restricted to EBV-PTLD, EBV-HLH, and chronic active EBV; not used in routine IM.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Etoposide selectively eliminates activated cytotoxic T cells driving the cytokine storm; central to EBV-HLH therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reserved for confirmed/strongly suspected EBV-HLH; not used in ordinary IM.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Useful adjunct in severe IM-associated ITP and AIHA refractory or in addition to corticosteroids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive in severe immune cytopenias of IM and in selected complicated cases.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Avoiding amoxicillin/ampicillin/aminopenicillins (and being cautious with cephalosporins) in suspected IM eliminates the classical drug-rash mechanism without compromising care.

failure_modes: misdiagnosis as streptococcal pharyngitis leading to inadvertent prescription
treatments.context_specific_role: Default rule when IM is suspected; if bacterial pharyngitis coinfection is confirmed, prefer penicillin V or, in non-severe penicillin allergy, a non-aminopenicillin alternative.

young_child_under_5.trajectory_modulation: Often subclinical or mild, atypical presentation; lower heterophile sensitivity (<50%).

adolescent_young_adult_15_to_24.trajectory_modulation: Peak incidence of clinically apparent IM; classical symptomatic course.

older_adult_over_40.trajectory_modulation: Less classic — fever and hepatitis often more prominent, lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis less prominent; higher rate of jaundice.

ebv_seronegative_susceptible.trajectory_modulation: Required substrate — primary EBV infection in seronegative host produces classic IM.

ebv_seropositive_past_infection.trajectory_modulation: Reactivation rarely produces an IM-like syndrome in immunocompetent hosts.

no_known_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Most cases lack identifiable contact (asymptomatic shedding by carriers).

post_transplant_or_chemotherapy.trajectory_modulation: Markedly elevated risk of fulminant hepatitis, EBV-HLH, and EBV-PTLD; routine IM picture is uncommon.

primary_immunodeficiency_xlp.trajectory_modulation: Catastrophic primary EBV — fulminant IM, HLH, dysgammaglobulinemia, lymphoma; fatal without HSCT.

hiv_advanced.trajectory_modulation: Higher risk of oral hairy leukoplakia, EBV-LPD, and CNS lymphoma.

amoxicillin_or_ampicillin_within_10_days.trajectory_modulation: Adds a strong drug-mediated rash component that masquerades as IM exanthem; high diagnostic clue when exudative pharyngitis is mistaken for strep.

supportive_care: Adequate oral hydration with cool fluids; consider IV fluids if odynophagia limits intake.
Acetaminophen first-line; ibuprofen for additional analgesia/antipyresis when bleeding risk is acceptable.
Saltwater gargles, throat lozenges, and topical anesthetic preparations for sore throat relief.
Strict avoidance of contact sports, vigorous physical activity, and abdominal trauma for at least 3-4 weeks from symptom onset (longer if splenomegaly persists), because of splenic rupture risk.
Avoid aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin) and use cephalosporins cautiously when IM is suspected to prevent the classical morbilliform drug eruption.
Counsel about expected duration: pharyngitis 1-2 weeks, fever 1-2 weeks, fatigue often weeks-months; gradual return to school/work and activity as tolerated.

Education on warning signs requiring urgent evaluation: severe abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain (splenic rupture), worsening dyspnea or stridor (airway obstruction), persistent jaundice, severe bleeding/petechiae, persistent fever beyond 3 weeks, or new neurologic symptoms.
Outpatient follow-up at 1-2 weeks with reassessment of organomegaly, transaminases when initially abnormal, and CBC if cytopenias were present.
In hospitalized or atypical cases, monitor ferritin/triglycerides/fibrinogen trends and lower the threshold for HLH workup if fever persists with rising ferritin or worsening cytopenias.

Consider corticosteroids only for impending airway obstruction, severe immune cytopenias, neurologic complications, fulminant hepatitis, or as part of HLH-directed therapy — not for routine symptom relief.
Reassure patients about the post-viral fatigue trajectory and avoid premature labeling as chronic fatigue syndrome; recommend graded activity rather than prolonged bed rest.
